claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure containing dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Internal lamellar or colony boundaries obstruct dislocations and promote dislocation pile-ups in the untreated alloy.
Dislocation pile-ups at the internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations and premature microcracking.
A trace boron addition of approximately 0.1–0.5 at% is the proposed intervention.
Boron will preferentially segregate to internal lamellar interfaces.
Boron segregation will modify the chemistry of the lamellar interfaces.
Boron segregation will lower the energy barrier for dislocation transmission across the interfaces.
Boron addition will reduce mismatch and local stress concentration at interlamellar interfaces by making them more coherent and less obstructive.
The modified interfaces will weaken the tendency for dislocation pile-ups and facilitate smoother dislocation motion across phase boundaries.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups and interfacial stress concentrations will delay microcrack initiation during deformation.
Boron-treated material will have greater room-temperature elongation to failure than untreated material.
Boron-treated material will maintain or slightly increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to untreated material.
The predicted benefit applies to room-temperature tensile loading at typical laboratory strain rates.
The beneficial composition range is limited by the onset of brittle boride precipitation.
Performance of the boron-modified alloy at elevated temperatures is unverified.
The magnitude of ductility enhancement and strength retention depends on boron concentration and interfacial distribution.
Exceeding boron's solubility limit may form brittle secondary phases and degrade performance.
